newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business - June 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business - June 17.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BRUSSELS MAY INVESTIGATE WINDFALL TAX

European Union competition commissioner Karel van Miert has warned that the Commission may end up scrutinising the British government's proposed windfall tax on the privatised utilities. Speaking in London, van Miert threatened that any discrimination in the way the tax was structured would give EU authorities cause to investigate.
-- FULL CIRCLE 2.5 MILLION STG IN RED AFTER LOSSES AT SAMSON

Kitchens and bathrooms group Full Circle has reported an increase in annual losses to 2.53 million stg from 645,000 stg. The losses included a 633,000 stg provision for losses at Samson Stairs, which is due to be closed or sold off after losing its main customer. Full Circle was rescued three years ago by former Spring Ram chiefs Bill Rooney and Alan Bell.
-- PLYSU'S TO GAIN FROM MOVE TO PLASTIC CARTONS

Container manufacturer Plysu is set to benefit from the preference of consumers for plastic bottles of milk rather than cartons. With supermarkets due to phase out cartons over the past 18 months, Plysu finance director Stephen Nobbs anticipates 'further growth in the dairy market, particularly for the plastic one-pinters'. Plysu reported a 34 percent increase in profits to 9.3 million stg.
THE TIMES
-- WINDFALL WHIRLWIND SWEEPS NORWICH AND NATIONWIDE

The windfall benefits to investors of the demutualisation which is sweeping through the financial services sector are gathering pace. Insurer Norwich Union paid out a minimum of 1,000 pounds stg to 1.8 million policyholders on Monday, the first day of trading of its shares. The Nationwide, now Britain's largest building society and publicly committed to mutual status, has acted to raise the minimum investment on its accounts. And predictions of the likely opening price of shares in the Woolwich next month have suggested a minimum windfall of 1,494 pounds stg for members.
-- BECKETT ACCUSES US ON AVIATION AID

Trade secretary Margaret Beckett has called for a response from the US after accusing it of infringing a 1992 trade agreement with Europe. Beckett claimed that US companies are receiving more government aid than is permitted under the trade agreement, and said that European aviation companies such as Airbus and British Aerospace are operating at a disadvantage because of this.
-- SAINSBURY'S TO OPEN ALL NIGHT

Supermarket group Sainsbury's is to introduce all-night opening to 25 of its stores from the end of this month. The 24-hour opening, which follows a lengthy trial in several Sainsbury stores nationwide, will affect 10 stores in London and 15 in cities and large towns around the country. Research by Sainsbury's found that over 50 percent of grocery shoppers favour 24-hour shopping.
THE GUARDIAN
-- KOHL'S COAL GRANTS 'UNFAIR'

The British government is backing calls for the European Union to ban subsidies to the German coal industry. An official complaint over the handouts has been lodged by Celtic Energy, the British company which is a leading producer of anthracite. The move, which has been supported by Welsh Office minister Peter Hain, comes as British companies find it difficult to break into European markets because German coal is being sold at below production costs.
-- POUND BUCKLES STEEL

British Steel has reported a 651 million stg collapse in pre-tax profits, to 451 million stg, and has announced plans to cut thousands of jobs and squeeze its suppliers. The results have been seen as one of the harshest demonstrations yet of the dangers of a strong pound, with currency accounting for 160 million stg of the profits fall. Announcing the results, BS chairman Sir Brian Moffat called on the government to raise taxes, not interest rates, to control inflation.
-- RESTAURANTEUR TO ROCK THE WEST END

Millionaire restauranteur Robert Earl is planning to open new themed restaurants in London and New York. Earl, who set up Planet Hollywood, has signed an agreement to lease 40,000 sq feet of space in New York's Times Square for the new rock music-based outlets. He is also planning a London version of his US sports-themed All Star Cafe, which is likely to be sited just off Leicester Square.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- HAWLEY QUITS BRITISH ENERGY WITH BUMPER 450,000 STG PAYOFF

William Hawley is to leave the post of chief executive at nuclear power generator British Energy. Hawley, 60, is to receive a pay-off of 450,000 pounds stg after he was refused the chairmanship of the privatised company. The board decided it wanted a younger man in the position, a decision which is likely to lead to further boardroom upheaval. BE has pledged to replace Hawley by the end of the year.
-- GEC TO CLOSE WORLD'S OLDEST TELECOMMUNICATIONS COLLEGE

Electronics giant GEC is to close its Marconi College, the world's oldest telecommunications training college. News of the planned closure of the Chelmsford-based college, which has been operating for over 90 years, has raised questions about the commitment of GEC to investment in education and training. GEC blamed the closure on falling orders for training from within GEC and from outside clients.
-- WARNING WIPES 73 MILLION STG OFF PSION

Computer group Psion saw its shares plunge 97.5p to 407.5p on Monday after it issued a warning that trading had been hit in advance of the launch of its new Series 5 computer. Psion also warned that the weakening of the German mark could hit margins; the group invoices 40 percent of its sales in D-Marks. The warning came as Psion launched Series 5, its new, state-of-the-art computer. Sales of Psion's Series 3 and Siena products have been subdued in anticipation of the newer product.
